en: Sutta Nipāta 1.3 Khaggavisāṇasutta:
“Having laid aside the rod toward all living beings,
Without harming even one among them,
one should not desire a son, much less a companion;
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“For one born of association, affections arise;
from these affections, this suffering comes into being.
Seeing the peril born of affection,”
“One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“Out of compassion for friends and companions,
one whose mind is bound to them lets go of his own welfare.”
Seeing this danger in intimacy,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Just as one who is clinging to a wide-spreading bamboo...
Regarding expectations for children and wives,
like the stalk of a bamboo, remaining unattached,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“Just as a deer, unbound in the forest,
goes wherever it wishes for its pasture;
so does a wise man, beholding freedom.”
“One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“There is an invitation in the midst of companions—
at home, in staying, in going, and on the journey.”
Beholding that which is unassailable and free from strife,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
"Amidst companions, there is play and delight."
And there is great affection for one's children;
loathing the separation from those dear,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
He is impartial toward the four quarters and free from resentment,
content with whatever comes his way;
enduring all hardships, he remains undaunted.
“One should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
“Some who have gone forth are difficult to support,
as are householders living at home.”
“Being unconcerned with the children of others,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having cast off the insignia of a householder,
Like a *koviḷāra* tree with its leaves stripped away,
having severed the bonds of household life,
let the hero wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“If one should find a prudent companion,
a steadfast friend who lives virtuously and walks together with one;
having overcome all dangers, [one may wander with him].”
One should practice with a mind delighted and mindful.
"If one does not find a wise companion to walk with— one who is steadfast, virtuous in conduct, and intelligent— "
"Like a king abandoning his conquered kingdom,
one should wander alone like an elephant in the Matanga forest.
"Truly, we praise the excellence of companionship," [said the others].
One should cultivate excellent companions;
failing to find such, one who eats blameless food should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“Having seen two [bracelets] of radiant gold,
well-finished by a smith’s son,
clashing against each other upon his arm,”
“One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“In this way, there would be conversation or even provocation with a companion;”
Foreseeing this danger in the future,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
For sensual pleasures are variegated, sweet, and delightful;
They churn one's mind with hideous forms;
having seen the danger in the strands of sensual pleasure,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“Calamity, tumor, and affliction,
disease, arrow, and fear— this is what [lies] within the strands of sensual pleasure. Having seen this danger, [one should abandon them].”
“One should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
Cold and heat, hunger and thirst,
wind and sun, and gadflies and snakes—
Having overcome all these,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Like an elephant avoiding the herds, one should go alone.
With shoulders well-rounded, lotus-like, and magnificent,
dwelling in the forest as long as you desire,
you should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“It is impossible for one who delights in company to experience temporary liberation,
even if they were to heed the words of the Kinsman of the Sun.”
“One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having transcended the thicket of views,
having attained the fixed course and found the path, he wanders alone.
“I have attained knowledge and am no longer led by others;
let me wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“Free from greed, free from deceit, free from thirst...”
Free from hypocrisy, with delusion and impurities burnt away,
and having become free from all longing for the entire world,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“One should avoid an evil companion,
one who sees no harm and is intent on what is wrong;
one should not associate with one who is addicted to and negligent in sensual pleasures.”
“One should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
One should associate with one who is learned, who upholds the Dhamma,
who is a sublime friend, and who is eloquent.
“Having understood the meanings and dispelled doubt,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“Play, delight, and sensual pleasure in the world...”
Without adorning himself, without longing,
detached from the means of adornment, a speaker of truth—
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“Having abandoned son, wife, father, and mother,
wealth, grain, and kinsmen, as well as all superfluous sensual pleasures, [one should go forth].”
“One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“This is a bond; here there is but little happiness, little gratification, and much suffering.”
"Knowing that this is a fetter, the wise one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros,
having torn asunder the fetters."
Like a water-dweller breaking through a net,
like a fire that does not turn back from what it has consumed,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
With downcast eyes and not fickle of foot,
with guarded sense-faculties and protected mind,
uncorrupted and without burning fever—
“One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having cast off the marks of a householder,
like the *pārichatta* tree with its dense foliage, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Clad in saffron robes, having gone forth,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Not greedy for flavors, not lustful...
Not supporting others, wandering from house to house in regular succession,
with a mind unattached to family after family,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“Having abandoned the five hindrances of the mind,
having dispelled all mental defilements,
being independent and having severed the fault of attachment— ”
“One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having turned one’s back on both pleasure and pain,
as well as prior joy and grief;
Having attained equanimity and purified tranquility,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
With energy aroused for the attainment of the supreme goal...
With a mind undaunted and conduct untiring,
with firm exertion and endowed with strength and power,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“Not neglecting seclusion and meditative absorption,
always practicing in accordance with the Dhamma regarding all phenomena,
and contemplating the peril in states of existence— ”
One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Striving for the destruction of craving, heedful,
not dull-witted, learned, and mindful.
One who has mastered the Dhamma, is certain,
and exerts himself— let him wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Like a lion, undaunted by sounds...
Like the wind not caught in a net,
like a lotus unsoiled by water,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Just as a lion, powerful with its fangs,
moves about having overcome the deer by force,
so should one frequent remote lodgings.
“One should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
Cultivating at the proper times loving-kindness, equanimity, compassion, liberation, and sympathetic joy.”
“Unopposed by the entire world,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion...
Having torn asunder the fetters,
remaining unafraid at the end of life,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
People resort to and serve others for the sake of some purpose;
friends without motive are rare these days.
Human beings are impure, perceiving only their own self-interest.
“One should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
The Rhinoceros Horn Sutta, the third.
